header: Present: Mr. Naeem Ahmad Khattak, Advocate for
Mr. Aimal Khan Barkandi, Advocate for
body: ************ BABAR SATTAR, J.- The petitioner has impugned (i) order dated 22.05.2024 dismissing an application filed by the petitioner in terms of Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (“CPC”), seeking the setting aside of ex-parte judgment and decree dated 26.11.2022, and (ii) the order of the Additional District Court dated 19.09.2024, dismissing the appeal against the order of the Civil Court. And in further relief, the petitioner has also sought setting aside of ex-parte judgment and decree dated 26.11.2022, pursuant to which the suit filed by the respondent for recovery of damages in the amount of Rs. 8 million on account of malicious prosecution and mental torture etc, was decreed in favour of the respondent.

2. The learned counsel for the petitioner took the court through the background facts and the record. He submitted that the impugned order passed by the Civil Court afforded no opportunity to the petitioner to produce evidence in support of his claim that the petitioner could not appear before the Civil Court due to illness and the petitioner's counsel was out of the country, which caused a delay in filing an application for setting aside the ex-parte judgment and decree. He submitted that the Additional District Court also upheld the order of the Civil Court without considering that judgments ought to be passed on merits and not on the basis of technicalities. He submitted that the impugned orders had consequently merged in ex-parte judgment and decree dated 26.11.2022 and the Additional District Court ought to have considered the infirmity in such ex-parte judgment and decree. He argued that the ingredients for grant of damages on account of malicious prosecution were not made out by the respondent and further that the respondent had not quantified and proved damages. He submitted that even in ex-parte proceedings, the claimant has to stand on his own feet and cannot draw any benefit due to the absence of the defendant. He submitted that as damages had not been proved, a decree that was devoid of reasoning and granted the claimant complete damages as claimed, without proof of sustaining such damages, could not be allowed to stand.

3. Learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the conduct of the petitioner before the Civil Court was contumacious. He submitted that during the first round, the Civil Court noted in order dated 03.10.2018 that despite the petitioner having been informed telephonically, he failed to appear before the Civil Court and was therefore proceeded against ex-parte. After recording of evidence, the Civil Court passed an ex-parte judgment and decree dated 12.11.2018. This judgment and decree was set aside by the Additional District Court and the matter was remanded back to the Civil Court. The petitioner then filed his written statement and thereafter disappeared once again. The civil court in view of the evidence produced by the respondent and considering the testimony of four plaintiff's witnesses, rendered a judgment and decree in favour of the respondent. He submitted that the respondent had established through evidence that he had filed an application and sought details with regard to the material being used in a construction project been undertaken by the Communication and Works Department of the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa at Maskeen Abad Judge Bungalow. At the time, the respondent was working as a university employee and had to file a request for information application for such purpose. As a counter blast to such application, whereby it had been directed that the requisite information be provided to the respondent, the petitioner had a false complaint recorded against the respondent on the basis of which, an FIR was registered and the respondent was arrested. The respondent then filed an application under Section 249-A of Cr.P.C, which was allowed and the respondent was acquitted of the charge of stealing old pipes that constituted public property. The respondent also established that the petitioner had published his allegations in Roznama Mashriq that inflicted reputational harm on the respondent. As a consequence of such events, the respondent lost his job and due to the emotional and financial pressure brought upon the respondent, his mother fell ill and had to be treated medically. It was in this backdrop that the respondent issued a notice to the petitioner and then filed a suit for malicious prosecution, which was decreed in view of the testimonies of the four witnesses (including the respondent himself) who testified in support of the claims of the respondent. He submitted that the Civil Court and the Additional District Court had correctly dismissed the application for setting aside the ex-parte decree in view of the fact that not a shred of material was produced by the petitioner to either establish that the petitioner could not appear before the Civil Court due to illness or that the petitioner's counsel was out of the country resulting in a delay in seeking the setting aside of ex-parte judgment and decree dated 26.11.2022. He submitted that the application was filed on 18.11.2023 which was rightly dismissed for being barred by limitation.

4. The facts in relation to the filing and dismissal of the application under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC are not contested. The respondent sued for damages for malicious prosecution. The suit was first decreed ex-parte on 12.11.2018. In appeal, the appellate court set that decree aside and remanded the matter. On remand the defendant filed a written statement and then stopped appearing and was again proceeded against ex-parte. The plaintiff examined four witnesses and claimed Rs. 8 million as damages for losses that he suffered. The trial court decreed the suit on 26.11.2022. Almost one year later, on 18.11.2023, the petitioner applied under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC seeking that the ex-parte decree be set aside. The trial court dismissed the application as time-barred and for want of sufficient cause, both for non-appearance of the petitioner and for the delay in filing of the application. The appellate court affirmed the order of the Civil Court.

5. The petitioner contends that he ought to have been granted an opportunity to adduce evidence in support of his application under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC. He further contends that the decree cannot stand because the plaintiff never proved the quantum of damages and that the plaintiff must prove his case on its own merits even when the defendant is absent. The decree holder argues that his evidence remained unrebutted and was rightly accepted. And that once Order IX, Rule 13 application was properly dismissed, the merits of the decree and the quantum of damages are no longer open for consideration before this Court in revision. The questions that arise for decision are the following:

i. Do the concurrent findings on sufficient cause and limitation under Order IX, Rule 13 disclose any jurisdictional defect, illegality or material irregularity that ought to be interfered with by this Court in exercise of its revision jurisdiction under Section 115 of CPC?
ii. In a revision arising from the dismissal of an application under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC, can the High Court examine the merits of the ex-parte decree, including the quantum of damages?

6. An application filed under Order IX, Rule 13, succeeds only if the defendant satisfies the Court that summons were not duly served or that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was fixed for hearing. And in doing so, applies within a period of 30 days of the issuance of the judgment and decree. This limit flows from Article 164 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908. Where summons are not duly served, the time runs from the date when the applicant acquires knowledge of the decree. In the instant case, the petitioner had appeared before the Civil Court and had filed a written statement. Consequently, the question of non-service of summons does not arise. And the 30-day limit for filing of an application under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC runs from the date of the decree. The application filed by the petitioner on 18.11.2023, seeking the setting aside of an ex-parte judgment and decree dated 26.11.2022 was plainly beyond time.

7. The application itself does not detail what sufficient cause prevented the petitioner from filing the application within the 30-day period. The first assertion made by the petitioner in his application was that the petitioner was ill and could therefore not appear before the court. The petitioner, however, produced no material or details of such illness preventing him from appearing before the Court or from filing an application under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC within time. The application further asserted that the petitioner's counsel was out of the country. Once again, no details of where the petitioner's counsel was, when he left the country and when he returned, were appended with the application. It was in view of the absolute lack of material establishing sufficient cause of disappearance of the petitioner or his inability to file an application for setting aside the ex-parte judgment and decree within time that the Civil Court rightly dismissed such application and the Additional District Court upheld such decision.

8. It is by now well settled that the right to due process and fair trial does not benefit the indolent. Article 10A of the Constitution guarantees the right of due process to both parties. Where a defendant obdurately refuses to face the Court and the claims brought by a claimant, and seeks delaying tactics to frustrate adjudication of the claims, he cannot turn back subsequently and argue that the claims be decided on merit without showing that he had a plausible cause for being unable to appear before the Court during trial proceedings. Even a strong case on merits does not excuse the unexplained absence of a defendant. In the facts of the present case, the history of when the suit was filed and how the petitioner's absence before the Court led to two rounds of proceedings before the Civil Court, resulting into the ex-parte judgment and decree dated 26.11.2022, is a matter of record. It is also evident from record that it was only after the execution proceedings were initiated and the respondent sought to recover from the petitioner that the application for setting aside ex-parte judgment and decree was filed on 18.11.2023, almost one year after the issuance of the exparte judgment and decree.

9. The learned counsel for the petitioner has failed to establish that the petitioner was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing before the Civil Court and that the application filed under Order IX, Rule 13 was within time. The Civil Court as well as the Additional District Court had considered the relevant facts and then dismissed the application filed by the petitioner. The findings are concurrent and are supported by record. Learned counsel for the petitioner has failed to establish that the impugned orders are a product of misreading or non-reading of evidence or suffer from a jurisdictional error. Consequently, there exists no ground in terms of Section 115 of CPC for this court to interfere with the impugned orders.

10. The next question that arises is whether the merits of the ex-parte judgment and decree dated 26.11.2022 can be examined by this Court in the instant case. The law in this regard is also fairly settled. A defendant against whom an ex-parte decree is passed has two concurrent and independent remedies. Such defendant can file an application under order IX, Rule 13 seeking that the decree be set aside if he can establish sufficient cause. Alternatively, such defendant can file an appeal against the decree under Section 96(2) of the CPC. The two remedies operate in separate domains. A party which chooses one remedy and fails cannot be allowed to employ proceedings under Section 115 of the CPC to obtain, as a consequence of rejection of a remedy sought under Order IX, Rule 13 of the CPC, what could have been sought through a remedy under Section 96(2) of the CPC.

11. In the petition before this Court, “a case which has been decided by any court subordinate to this High Court”, for the purposes of Section 115 of the CPC, is the case brought by the petitioner before the Civil Court pursuant to his application under Order IX, Rule 13 of the CPC. The only relevant legal question arising therefrom was that related to whether the petitioner had satisfied the Court that he was prevented by “sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing”. That question has been addressed by the Civil Court and the Appellate Court, and no illegality or jurisdictional defect in relation to such finding has been made out before this Court. Whether the ex-parte judgment and decree dated 26.11.2022 were sustainable, or whether such decision suffered from any illegality or irregularity, is not a question that arises from the “case decided” from which the present revision petition has arisen. A revision cannot be used to examine a judgment and decree on its merits against which an appeal was available but not filed. Section 115 of CPC clearly provides that a revision lies in a case which has been decided by a subordinate Court from which no appeal lies.

12. The question of what constitutes a “case” for the purposes of Section 115 of the CPC, and how the doctrine of merger operates in relation to the judgment and decree of the trial Court and the appellate Court, is settled.

13. In S. Zafar Ahmad Vs. Abdul Khaliq, (PLD 1964 (W.P.) Karachi 149), a Full Bench laid down guidelines for exercise of revisional jurisdiction and how such jurisdiction is fundamentally distinguishable from appellate jurisdiction. It was held that, “Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not concern itself directly with justice or injustice. It is not a power to substitute what appears to the revisional Court to be correct view of the merits of a case--whether legal or factual---for a view of the merits of the case that appears to it to be erroneous. Section 115 is not concerned with these matters. It is, on the contrary, concerned only with the exercise of jurisdiction. If no jurisdiction that is not vested is exercised; if no jurisdiction that is vested, no one has acted illegally or with material irregularity, the question of using powers under Section 115 does not arise, however, gross an error of law or fact might have been committed in the determination of the merits of the claim and however grave the injustice might be.”

14. In Umar Dad Khan Vs. Tila Muhammad Khan, (PLD 1970 Supreme Court 288), the Supreme Court reiterated that while the term “case decided” did not necessarily refer to a final judgment in the case, not every interlocutory order would be interfered with by the High Court in its revisional jurisdiction. The Supreme Court noted that, “we appreciate the anxiety of the learned judges to correct an error which has occurred in the trial of a suit. This, however, does not justify transgressing the boundaries of their jurisdiction vested by law.”

15. In Atul Chandra Das Vs. Bhagbati Das, (PLD 1967 Dacca 27), it was highlighted that, “an application under Order IX, Rule 13, is sui generis and has no nexus with an appeal filed against an ex-parte decree or with a review application, in respect of the same subject-matter, under Order XLVII of the Code of Civil Procedure. These are independent and, often, concurrent remedies which are available to an aggrieved party.”

It was further noted that, “the principle that an original decree is merged in an appellate decree is wellsettled. But it does not solve the problem which confronts us… It is true that the original decree loses its identity in the appellate decree which supplants the original decree and wipes out its existence. But, the right conferred under Order IX, Rule 13, is of a different nature, namely, a right by a party who has not at all been heard in respect of the decree that has been passed against such party to apply to the trial Court to set aside the decree. It is a right specially conferred by law without which no such right could have existed. It is a statutory relief of a special kind arising out of the mandate of law.”

While explaining that the filing of an appeal did not exhaust the jurisdiction of the trial Court to entertain an application under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC, it was held that, “an application under Order IX, Rule 13, being a remedy, which is sui generis, is maintainable on the strength of the very provisions of law which created the remedy.

It is not dependent upon any other extraneous consideration. On principle as well as on authority, it seems, that the trial Court was competent to entertain the application. But, when the party making the application under Order IX, Rule 13, has had a full chance of agitating the points which he intended to canvass in the trial Court, no life can subsist in his application under Order IX, Rule 13, for the simple reason that he has had his case fully heard and decided by a competent Court, namely, the appellate Court, the Court sitting in appeal over the original decree.”

16. It was held by the Supreme Court in Ibrahim Vs. Mst. Kulsoom Begum, (1973 SCMR 589), that, “Under Order XLIII, Rule 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure an appeal lies from an order under Rule 13 of Order IX of the Code rejecting an application (in a case open to appeal) for an order to set aside a decree ex-parte. In view of the aforesaid provisions of law once an ex-parte decree has been passed against a defendant he has two alternatives before him, namely-(1) either make an application under Order IX, Rule 13 of the Code for setting aside the ex-parte decree and in case he is unsuccessful an appeal under Order XLIII, Rule 1(d) of the Code is available to him, or (2) he may prefer an appeal under Section 96, subsection (2) of the Code.”

17. What emerges from the above is that where an application under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC has been dismissed, and the appeal against such order has also been dismissed, the matter would constitute a “case decided” for purposes of Section 115 of the CPC, against which a revision lies. However, the case decided relates to the merits of the decisions rendered in an application under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC and not the merits of the ex-parte judgment and decree passed by the Civil Court. The doctrine of merger applies such that the order of the Civil Court in dismissing the application under Order IX, Rule 13, merges with the order of the appellate Court under Order XLIII, Rule 1(d) of CPC dismissing such appeal. Such orders of the Civil Court and the appellate Court, however, do not merge with the ex-parte judgment and decree, against which an appeal is provided under Section 96 of CPC, but has not been filed. Consequently, in revision, it is not the merits of the ex-parte judgment and decree that are before the High Court, but the merits of the order in relation to the application under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC.

18. Learned counsel for the petitioner relied on case law to argue that this Court was vested with wide suo motu powers that could be exercised under Section 115 of CPC. Learned counsel for the petitioner is not incorrect in arguing that the High Court can call for the record of any case that has been decided by any Court subordinate to it. However, exercise of such power still remains subject to the condition that no appeal lies against such order. And further that the order of the subordinate Court satisfies the conditions prescribed under sub-clauses (a), (b) or (c) of Section 115(1) of CPC. Such powers are exercised extremely sparingly and are ordinarily reserved for instances where the orders are found to be void or without jurisdiction. A decree by a Court of competent jurisdiction, passed after the recording of evidence, is not void merely because the findings of such Court on the question of liability or the question of damages is argued to be unreasoned. Such an error would constitute an error of law or fact within the jurisdiction of the Court, liable to be corrected in appeal. To exercise suo motu powers in the facts of the present case to set aside an ex-parte judgment and decree passed by the Civil Court against which no appeal was filed before the District Court, would be tantamount to rewarding the petitioner's conduct that the Civil Court and the Additional District Court condemned in the judgments that have been impugned before this Court. If this were to be allowed, a party who stayed away from the trial proceedings, delaying adjudication of the counterparty's claims and let the limitation periods prescribed for an Order IX, Rule 13 application, as well as the limitation period for purposes of appeal lapse, would end up obtaining in revision a review of the merits that could be challenged in appeal, which opportunity the party forfeited.

19. If this Court were to engage with the petitioner’s arguments on the merits of the ex-parte judgment and decree and were to come to the conclusion that either the constituent elements in a case for malicious prosecution were not made out or that there existed no proof of damages without which the respondent's claim for damages could not be sustained, this Court would be faced with two competing principles: On the one hand, a chronically defaulting litigant should not be rewarded for his indolence; and, on the other hand, should the strict application of procedural law allow an unreasoned decree to stand as a valid judicial instrument? The petitioner's best argument on the merits of the ex-parte judgment and decree is that the judgment is unreasoned and grants damages that were not quantified. Even if such arguments were to be accepted as being meritorious, which would tantamount to errors in the reasoning of the Civil Court, they would still not take the decision of the Civil Court outside its jurisdiction.

20. Such arguments can only be considered in an appropriate case where they arise in a case that the High Court can assume jurisdiction over in terms of Section 115 of CPC. The counterargument is not without merit. The finality of a decision rendered upon culmination of trial proceedings is not a mere technicality. The law of limitation is an embodiment of public policy that supports certainty and finality. Once a judicial decision becomes final, it creates rights in favour of the winner as a product of an adversarial process. If the High Court were to re-open the merits of an ex-parte judgment and decree in a case where no appeal was filed and the case that comes before the High Court arises from dismissal of an application under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC and the dismissal of an appeal against such order, it could open another avenue for a defaulter staying away from trial and appellate proceedings, and then opening up the entire Pandora’s box under the restrictive jurisdiction vested in the High Court in terms of Section 115 of CPC. While procedure must always remain the handmaiden of justice, depriving a claimant of the benefits of a judgment and decree that has otherwise attained finality, in a collateral attack brought forth under Section 115 of the CPC, after dismissal of an Order IX Rule 13 application and the appeal against such order would also do no service to the cause of justice.

21. For the above reasons, this court finds that the only question before the Court in its present jurisdiction relates to the merits of the petitioner’s application under Order IX, Rule 13 of CPC, which has been dismissed through concurrent findings of the Civil Court and the Additional District Court, and, as held above, has been found to suffer from no illegality or jurisdictional defect. Without touching the merits of the respondent’s claim and the merits of the ex-parte judgment and decree, which do not arise from the case decided from which the present revision emanates, this court finds that the petition is without merit and is dismissed.
Announced 03.11.2026 *Asif Jan CO* JUDGE *SB* Hon’ble Mr. Justice Babar Sattar, J.
